steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a side-by-side look at the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Full name  
   • DNA: Deoxyribonucleic acid  
   • RNA: Ribonucleic acid

2. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA: deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group at the 2′ carbon)  
   • RNA: ribose (has an –OH at the 2′ carbon)

3. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T)  
   • RNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), uracil (U) instead of thymine

4. Strand structure  
   • DNA: usually double-stranded, forming a stable helix  
   • RNA: usually single-stranded, can fold into complex 3D shapes

5. Location in the cell  
   • DNA: confined mainly to the nucleus (eukaryotes) or nucleoid (prokaryotes)  
   • RNA: synthesized in the nucleus but functions throughout the cytoplasm (and in organelles)

6. Main functions  
   • DNA: long-term storage of genetic information (the “blueprint” for all proteins)  
   • RNA: diverse roles, including  
     – messenger RNA (mRNA): carries coding instructions from DNA to ribosomes  
     – transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis  
     – ribosomal RNA (rRNA): core component of ribosomes  
     – regulatory RNAs (e.g. miRNA, siRNA) and catalytic RNAs (ribozymes)

7. Chemical stability  
   • DNA: more chemically stable (no 2′–OH), ideal for archival storage  
   • RNA: less stable (2′–OH can hydrolyze), suitable for transient messages and dynamic regulation

8. Length and abundance  
   • DNA: very long (entire genome), exists as a few large molecules (chromosomes)  
   • RNA: generally shorter, many different species and copies per cell

Summary  
DNA is the stable, double-stranded repository of genetic information, built on deoxyribose and using thymine. RNA is a versatile, usually single-stranded molecule built on ribose and using uracil, acting as the active intermediary (and sometimes regulator or catalyst) in decoding and using the information stored in DNA.
